newsitem.title: USA: Swift currents still a threat on lower Mississippi.
newsitem.headline: Swift currents still a threat on lower Mississippi.

text.p: Swift currents continued to play havoc with maritime traffic on the lower Mississippi, Coast Guard officials said, causing yet another barge accident on the river early Tuesday.
Although water levels were gradually subsiding on the lower half of the river, navigation conditions remained hazardous, officials said.
The Coast Guard was forced to halt maritime traffic near New Orleans for 90 minutes early Tuesday after a breakaway barge collided with a fleeting facility just south of the city.

"Traffic was interrupted for a short period (but) is back open now," said Commander Daniel Whiting of the Coast Guard's Marine Safety Office in New Orleans. No injuries or spills occurred as a result of the accident, he added.
Meanwhile, salvage operations were continuing on a chemical freighter that was damaged in a collision just outside the river in the Gulf of Mexico over the weekend.

The Formosa Six collided late Saturday with a bulk carrier, the Flora, two miles outside of the Southwest Pass. An unknown quantity of ethylene dichloride from the Formosa Six spilled into the water, but officials said maritime transit in the area was not affected by the incident.
"It is not restricting traffic outside the Southwest Pass," Whiting said. "The vessel is stable and at anchorage. Our goal is to keep the vessel stable in its present location."

The lower Mississippi has been plagued by shipping accidents for several weeks, as raging floodwaters make the river difficult to navigate. Safety regulations imposed last month would remain in place until further notice.

In addition to draft restrictions at the mouth of the river in Southwest Pass, the Coast Guard was sticking to a daytime-only restricion on all southbound, deep-draft vessels carrying chemicals or compressed gases. Minimum power requirements for barge tows would also be maintained, officials said.

Water levels dropped to around 15.8 feet in New Orleans on Tuesday, down sharply from the river's 16.9 foot crest last week. The Coast Guard said renewed flooding this week in the upper Midwest could keep the lower river at unusually high levels for some time.
((-- W Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
